open-question.question: What is the file name of the new task-list tool under core/tools/, the name every runtime command, CLAUDE.md invariant, doc entry, and test fixture will carry (define_milestone.py and open_questions.py are the two existing precedents)?
open-question.recommendation: It is the name the goal, the pipeline summary, and the docs already use for the thing, a document-named noun after the open_questions.py precedent, where write_tasks.py names a generic act over verb subcommands, tasks.py is a generic module name drowned in every search, and task_lists.py is a rarer form one letter from a run-time typo in every fixed command.
open-question.alternative: Name the tool core/tools/task_list.py: a document-named noun in the open_questions.py style, singular, taken from the "task list" / "task-list tool" wording the milestone goal, the skill descriptions, and docs already use for TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md together. Every runtime command reads python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/task_list.py <subcommand> <MILESTONE_DIR> …, and tests and the conftest runner take the matching task_list prefix. It matches the vocabulary already in place: "task list" and "task-list" are the most frequent terms in core/ and docs/ for these files, and the milestone itself calls the thing the task-list tool, so the name needs no explanation in CLAUDE.md, the docs, or a skill step, and subcommands like move, insert, and append read naturally after a noun, as they do after open_questions.py. The singular names one list while the tool writes two files, and "task list" in prose often means TASKS_TODO.md alone (complete-all-tasks works "the task list"), so the name slightly understates that the move spans both files.

Name the tool core/tools/task_lists.py: a document-named noun in the open_questions.py style, plural like open_questions.py, naming both task files the tool writes as the two task lists. Commands read python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/task_lists.py <subcommand> <MILESTONE_DIR> …, with tests and the conftest runner under the task_lists prefix. It mirrors the closest precedent exactly (a plural noun naming the documents the tool is the sole writer of, the subcommands carrying the verbs) and states in the name that one tool owns both TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md, which is what the sole-writer invariant in CLAUDE.md will say. "Task lists" is a rarer form in the existing prose than "task list", and task_list.py versus task_lists.py is an easy one-letter slip in the many fixed commands written into runtime prose, where a typo fails at run time rather than in the build.

Name the tool core/tools/tasks.py: a document-named noun taken from the TASKS_ prefix the two files share, the shortest form. Commands read python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/tasks.py <subcommand> <MILESTONE_DIR> …, with tests and the conftest runner under the tasks prefix. It ties the name directly to the file names it writes (TASKS_TODO.md, TASKS_DONE.md) and keeps every fixed command, including the long chained completion call shown in full in runtime prose, as short as possible. The word "tasks" is everywhere in the runtime prose, docs, and test names, so searching for the tool's call sites or test files by its name is noisy, and a bare tasks.py on the pytest pythonpath is a generic module name that says less about what the file is than either existing tool's name does.

Name the tool core/tools/write_tasks.py: an act-named verb_noun in the define_milestone.py style, the verb naming the tool's role as the only writer of the task files (reads stay prose, per the goal). Commands read python3 {{PLUGIN_ROOT}}/tools/write_tasks.py <subcommand> <MILESTONE_DIR> …, with tests and the conftest runner under the write_tasks prefix. The name itself carries the milestone's central claim, that this tool writes and nothing else does, and signals at every call site that reads of TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md do not go through it. define_milestone.py is a single-act tool with no subcommands, so this follows its form but not its shape: a verb name over verb subcommands reads doubled (write_tasks.py move, write_tasks.py insert), and a read subcommand added later, such as a heading listing, would contradict the name.

open-question.question: When the task-list tool is given a task title (the section to move, or a before/after anchor), does it match it exactly after whitespace- and case-folding, refusing anything else so a partial task name is resolved by the runner's own read of TASKS_TODO.md before the call, or does it carry the completion procedure's case-insensitive partial match itself, which then needs a rule for two sections matching and a way to tell the runner which heading it took?
open-question.recommendation: The tool keeps the open-question tool's folded-id comparison and silent-mutator contract while the partial-name convenience survives at no cost in step 1's whole read, which complete-all-tasks already bypasses by passing the exact heading; the tool-side partial forms resolve the name twice by two rules and two of them break the silent-mutator contract, and retiring the convenience widens the milestone for a problem the runner's read already solves.
open-question.alternative: The tool matches every title it is given (the section to move and a before/after anchor alike) against the `##` headings only by exact equality after whitespace-folding and case-folding, the open-question tool's id comparison; anything else, a partial name or two sections sharing the folded title included, is refused with one Error: line and both files unchanged. The completion procedure keeps its case-insensitive partial match in prose: step 1 resolves the user's partial name against its own whole read of TASKS_TODO.md (listing the headings on no match, as today) and the runner passes the full heading it located to the move. The tool prints nothing on success. Keeps the tool deterministic and its contract identical to open_questions.py (folded ids, silent mutator, one Error: line), while the partial-name convenience the inline /complete-task documents survives at no extra cost, since step 1 already reads TASKS_TODO.md whole and complete-all-tasks already passes the exact heading. Name resolution is split between prose and tool, so the runner must copy the located heading verbatim into the call and a heading it retypes differently in more than case or whitespace is refused after the work is done; a duplicated folded title in the file blocks the move entirely, which leans on title uniqueness, a condition the uniqueness-enforcement question owns.

The tool matches a title only when it equals a `##` heading's text byte for byte after trimming the line's ends, with no case- or inner-whitespace-folding, and refuses anything else with one Error: line and both files unchanged. The completion procedure keeps its partial match in prose and passes the exact heading it located; the tool prints nothing on success. The strictest and simplest rule: the title the tool matched is exactly the text that lands in the Task-completion: subject and in TASKS_DONE.md, with no comparison form to define or test. Breaks parity with the open-question tool's folded-id convention, so the workflow's two sole-writer tools compare titles differently, and a runner's harmless case or spacing slip in retyping a heading becomes a refused move.

The tool matches by exact equality after whitespace- and case-folding and refuses anything else, as in the first option, and the partial match is retired from the workflow altogether: complete-procedure.md step 1 also requires the given name to equal a heading after folding, the inline /complete-task's "full or partial text" argument contract becomes full text only, and a no-match still stops listing the available headings so the caller can retry. The tool prints nothing on success. One matching rule from the user's argument through step 1 to the tool, so the section the procedure read and the section the tool moves can never diverge, and the prose loses its loosest rule rather than merely relocating it. Takes away a documented convenience of the inline skill (typing a fragment of a long title) and widens the milestone's prose and doc edits to the skill's argument contract and docs/skill-reference.md, for a matching problem the runner's own read already solves.

alternative.id: Tool partial, refuse ambiguity, print heading

open-question.alternative: The tool carries the matching itself for the moved section and the anchors alike: an exact folded match wins when one exists, otherwise a case-insensitive substring match against the headings must be unique; two or more partial matches are refused with one Error: line naming the candidate headings and both files unchanged. On success the move prints the full heading it took on stdout, an exception to the rule that a mutator prints nothing, so the runner can use it in the commit subject. The completion procedure passes the user's name as given. Matching moves out of prose into tested code with a defined ambiguity rule, and the runner learns authoritatively which heading moved, so the subject and report cannot name a different task than the files record. Breaks the silent-mutator contract both existing tools hold, and step 1 still has to locate and read the section in prose before the work, so the name is resolved twice (prose at step 1, tool at step 5) by two rules that can disagree; a partial anchor can also land a submitted task beside the wrong section.

The tool carries the same exact-first, then unique case-insensitive substring match for the moved section and the anchors alike, refusing two or more partial matches with one Error: line naming the candidates and both files unchanged, and it prints nothing on success; the runner takes the heading for its commit subject and report from its own step-1 read of the section. Gains a tested, defined ambiguity rule in the tool while keeping the silent-mutator contract both existing tools share. The heading the runner reports comes from its prose read, not from the tool, so a disagreement between the prose resolution at step 1 and the tool's resolution at step 5 goes unseen, and the tool's partial matching duplicates work the runner has already done.

alternative.id: Tool partial, first match, print heading

open-question.alternative: The tool carries the matching for the moved section and the anchors alike: an exact folded match wins when one exists, otherwise the first heading in file order containing the name case-insensitively is taken, with no ambiguity refusal; on success the move prints the full heading it took on stdout so the runner can name it. Never refuses a name that matches something, mirroring the unstated first-hit behaviour runners exhibit today, and the printed heading tells the runner what was moved. A fragment shared by two titles silently moves or anchors on whichever comes first, and the runner learns of a wrong pick only after both task files have changed; it also breaks the silent-mutator contract.

alternative.id: Partial for move, exact for anchors

open-question.alternative: The rule differs by argument: the moved section's title is matched by the tool exact-first, then by a unique case-insensitive substring, two or more partial matches refused with one Error: line naming the candidates, while a before/after anchor is matched only by exact whitespace- and case-folded equality. The tool prints nothing on success and the runner takes the moved heading from its own step-1 read. Puts partial matching only where a human-typed name reaches the tool (the /complete-task argument) and keeps anchors, which submit-task chooses from its own read of the file, strict so an insert never lands beside a guessed section. Two matching rules in one tool for the same kind of value make its contract harder to state and test, and the move still resolves its name twice (prose and tool); how an anchor naming no section is handled stays a condition the unknown-anchor question owns.

open-question.question: In what form does the move subcommand read the derived acceptance bar on standard input: one criterion per non-empty line, criteria separated by blank lines so a criterion wrapped over several lines folds to one bullet, or already-rendered "- " bullets the tool checks and copies under the **Verified:** label?
open-question.recommendation: Every recorded bar since the split is one single-line bullet per criterion, so a line-per-criterion reading needs no folding rule and the tool owns the label and the bullet syntax as the goal asks; stripping one habitual leading marker costs a one-line test and keeps the first calls after the change from being refused on habit, where the strict form spends a turn, and the paragraph, verbatim, and JSON forms each trade a silent merge, an unchecked block, or an escaping burden for a problem the record shows does not occur.
open-question.alternative: Framing: one criterion per non-empty line, as in the strict form. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label and one "- " bullet per line. Strictness: lenient on the marker — a single leading "- " on a line is stripped before the tool adds its own, so bare lines and already-bulleted lines render identically; only an empty bar is refused. Accepts both what the new prose will ask for and what runners habitually write, so the move never fails on the marker and the rendered bullets are uniform either way, while the tool still owns the label and the bullet syntax. The contract has two accepted spellings, so the prose and the tests must cover both, and a criterion whose own text begins with "- " loses that prefix; a wrapped criterion still splits silently into two bullets.

Framing: the runner pipes the bare criteria with no bullet marker, one criterion per non-empty line; blank lines are ignored. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label and prefixes each line with "- ". Strictness: a line that already starts with "- " is refused with an Error: line and both files unchanged, so a double bullet never lands, and a stdin holding no criterion is refused. The simplest contract to state and test: one line is one criterion, the bullet syntax lives only in the tool, and every Verified block in milestones 28 to 45 is already exactly one single-line bullet per criterion, so it reproduces the recorded shape with no folding rule. Runners have always been shown the bar as "- " bullets in step 5's template and about 150 agents wrote it that way, so the first call after the change is likely to be refused until the prose retrains them; a criterion a runner wraps over two lines silently becomes two bullets, a split the tool cannot detect.

Framing: criteria are separated by blank lines, so each paragraph is one criterion and a criterion wrapped over several lines is folded, its lines joined with single spaces, into one bullet. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label and one "- " bullet per paragraph, stripping a single leading "- " from a paragraph if present. A long criterion (several in milestone 45 run well past a hundred words) can be wrapped freely in the heredoc and still lands as exactly one bullet, so line length never changes how many criteria are recorded. Every criterion needs a blank line after it, an unusual framing runners will not write by habit: a forgotten blank line silently merges two criteria into one bullet, a corruption no check can catch, which is worse than the split the line-based forms risk.

Framing: the runner pipes the bar already rendered as "- " bullets, one per line, exactly as step 5's template shows it today. Rendering: the tool checks and copies the bullets under the **Verified:** label it writes itself, normalizing only the surrounding blank lines. Strictness: every non-empty line must start with "- ", otherwise the call is refused with an Error: line and both files unchanged; an empty bar is refused. Matches what runners already write and what the recorded entries show, so the stdin a runner composes is literally the block the entry will hold; the check still catches stray prose, a pasted label, or an unbulleted line before anything is written. The bullet syntax stays in runtime prose, so the rendering only partly leaves it for the tool, and a criterion wrapped onto a continuation line is refused, costing the runner a corrected re-call.

Framing: "- " bullets as in the strict rendered form, but a non-empty line that does not start with "- " is read as a continuation of the bullet above it and folded into that bullet with a single space; a continuation line before the first bullet is refused. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label and one normalized single-line bullet per criterion. Accepts the habitual bullet form and tolerates wrapping, since a bullet marker, not a line break, starts a criterion, so a wrapped criterion lands as one bullet without the blank-line discipline the paragraph form needs. The most lenient parser to specify and test, and a criterion whose author forgot its "- " is silently merged into the previous one; the bullet syntax still lives in runtime prose.

Framing: stdin is opaque Markdown. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label, then the piped text verbatim with only its leading and trailing blank lines trimmed, then the separator. Strictness: none beyond refusing an empty bar — the tool neither splits criteria nor checks bullets. Nothing the runner writes is ever refused or reshaped, so nested bullets, multi-line criteria, or code spans survive exactly, and the tool's parsing is the smallest of any option. The one-bullet-per-criterion shape stays a prose convention the tool does not hold, so a malformed bar (prose paragraphs, a duplicated label) lands silently, and the goal's aim of moving the Verified rendering out of runtime prose is only half met.

Framing: stdin is a JSON array of strings, one string per criterion, parsed with the standard library. Rendering: the tool writes the **Verified:** label and one "- " bullet per string, folding any internal newline to a space. Strictness: anything that is not a non-empty array of non-empty strings is refused with an Error: line and both files unchanged. Completely unambiguous: criterion boundaries never depend on line breaks, blank lines, or markers, so neither a split nor a merge can happen silently. The runner must JSON-escape every double quote and backslash in criteria that routinely quote phrases and commands, an escaping burden runtime prose would have to teach and runners would get wrong, and it breaks the tools' convention of free text piped as a plain quoted heredoc.

open-question.question: Does the task-list tool parse a whole task file and re-render it in one canonical layout on every write, normalizing the blank-line convention of every section it did not touch, or does it splice only the bytes of the section it adds or removes and leave every other byte of the file as it stands?
open-question.recommendation: One render-then-replace path mirroring the open-question tool is deterministic, testable against golden fixtures, and makes the jammed-heading and doubled-blank seams impossible anywhere in the file, which converges on the documented layout after one write; the first-write churn on the three drifted files is one-time whitespace on finished milestones, refusing drift would stop a headless run on cosmetics, and both splice forms leave seams or drift the convention never converges on.
open-question.alternative: On every write (initialize, append, insert, move) the tool parses the whole task file into its heading line and its ## sections (title, body prose, and for a done entry the **Verified:** bullets), applies the change to that model, and renders the entire file in one canonical layout: a blank line after the heading, after the body, after the label, after the last bullet, after each ---, and the file ending in --- plus one newline. Every section the call did not touch is re-emitted in that layout too, so any blank-line drift in it is normalized silently on the first write; the body prose itself is carried through as parsed text. The file is replaced through the same-directory temporary file, as open_questions.py does. One write path that mirrors open_questions.py's render-then-replace, so output is deterministic and testable against golden fixtures, and the seam failures runners hit today (a milestone-45 agent ran a second script to restore the blank line between a --- and the next heading) cannot occur anywhere in the file, which converges on the documented convention after one write. The first write to a file that drifted (milestone_41 ends in an extra blank line, milestone_42 holds a double blank, milestone_30 lacks a blank after a separator) or that someone edited by hand rewrites sections the commit is not about, so the Task-completion or Task-submission diff carries unrelated whitespace churn; and the parser must round-trip every body shape (internal paragraph breaks, lists, fenced code with blank lines) or it alters content it was never asked to touch. How strict that parse is depends on the unterminated-section and format-validation axes the sibling questions own.

The tool parses and renders the whole file in the one canonical layout, as above, but before writing it re-renders the file as read and compares it to the bytes on disk: if the two differ, the call is refused with one Error: line naming the file and the files are left unchanged; only a file already in canonical form is written, through the same render-then-replace path. Initialization, which replaces the contents by design, is the one write not gated on the old bytes. Keeps the single deterministic render path and its testability while guaranteeing the tool never silently changes a byte of a section it was not asked to touch, so every task commit's diff is exactly the change made, and drift is surfaced the moment it appears instead of being absorbed. Any hand edit or historical drift that is not byte-canonical blocks every subsequent tool call on that file until someone fixes it by hand, which stops a headless complete-all-tasks run mid-milestone on a cosmetic difference; and body text the parser cannot round-trip exactly becomes a refusal rather than a write, so the parser's fidelity is load-bearing for availability.

The tool parses only to locate boundaries (the target section's ## line through its ---, or the anchor's position) and writes by splicing: a removal deletes exactly that byte span, an insertion or append places a canonically rendered new section at the located offset, and every other byte of the file, including the whitespace around the splice point, stays as it stands. No section, separator, or blank line outside the inserted or removed span is rewritten; the file is still replaced atomically through a same-directory temporary file. The tool changes nothing it was not asked to change, so diffs are minimal, hand-edited or drifted sections survive untouched, and the parser need only find headings and separators rather than model and round-trip every body shape. The new section inherits whatever whitespace its neighbour leaves, so a neighbour missing its trailing blank line yields a heading jammed against a --- (the exact repair a milestone-45 agent had to script), and removing a section can leave a double blank or none; layout consistency is not guaranteed, drift accumulates, and tests must cover splice offsets rather than one rendered form. Locating boundaries still depends on how the unterminated-section sibling resolves a section with no ---.

The tool keeps every byte of every untouched section exactly as it stands, as in a pure splice, but normalizes the whitespace at each junction its own write creates: an inserted or appended section gets exactly one blank line before its ## heading and one after its ---, and the gap a removed section leaves collapses to the single blank line the convention calls for, with the end of file normalized to --- plus one newline only when the write touched the end. Drift anywhere away from a junction is left in place. Combines a minimal diff and no silent rewriting of other sections with a guarantee that every seam the tool produces is well-formed, so the jammed-heading and doubled-blank failures cannot be introduced by a write even into a drifted file. It is a third behaviour with its own rules to specify and test (which whitespace counts as part of a seam, what happens at the file heading and at end of file), more logic than either a render or a raw splice, and it still leaves the file internally inconsistent wherever drift sits away from a junction, so the file never converges on the convention by itself.

open-question.question: When a task file holds a ## section with no trailing --- separator before the next ## heading or the end of the file, does the tool refuse the call with an Error: line and the files unchanged, or treat the next heading or the end of file as that section's end?
open-question.recommendation: The tool never guesses where a section ends and keeps the refuse-with-files-unchanged contract the open-question tool already holds for a malformed document; no post-split task file holds an unterminated section, so the case arises only from a hand edit against a sole-writer invariant and its fix is one separator line, whereas the tolerant readings silently move or re-render a half-pasted section and the touched-only form adds a second parse mode for the same file.
open-question.alternative: The tool parses every `##` section of each task file the call reads, and if any section in either file reaches the next `##` heading or the end of the file with no `---` line, it refuses the whole call with one `Error:` line naming that section's heading and the file. Both files are left byte-for-byte unchanged, whichever section the call was about. The `---` separator stays a mandatory part of the file format, enforced by the tool on every call. The tool never guesses where a section ends, so it can never fold a neighbouring section into a moved task or misplace an inserted one. This is the same refuse-with-the-document-unchanged contract the open-question tool already uses. The fault is reported the first time any write touches the file, before more sections are written around it. One hand-edited section anywhere in the file blocks every write to it, including a move of some other task, until someone fixes the file by hand. In the middle of `complete-all-tasks` that stops the whole run. In this repository only the pre-split `milestone_13` has such a section, so the case comes only from a hand edit, but when it happens it stops work that has nothing to do with the faulty section.

The tool refuses with one `Error:` line, both files unchanged, only when the unterminated section is one the call has to cut or place against: the section being moved, the section named as a `before:`/`after:` anchor, or the last section of a file the call appends to. An unterminated section the call does not touch is tolerated: its end is taken to be the next `##` heading or the end of the file, and the tool does not add the missing `---`. The tool still never has to guess about any section it actually writes around. A stray hand edit somewhere else in the file does not block unrelated moves or insertions, so `complete-all-tasks` and `submit-task` keep going until the faulty section itself is reached. Every subcommand needs two parse modes, strict for the touched sections and lenient for the rest. That adds a rule to the tool's contract and its tests, and it lets an unterminated section stay in the file unnoticed until a later call reaches it. Whether an untouched section can stay byte-for-byte as it stands depends on the whole-file-rewrite-or-splice axis, which a sibling question owns.

The tool takes a section's end to be its `---` line if one comes first, and otherwise the next `##` heading or the end of the file. Any call involving an unterminated section succeeds and prints nothing, as the mutator contract requires. Every section the tool writes or moves, including an entry it appends to `TASKS_DONE.md`, gets its `---`. When an insertion lands directly behind an unterminated section, the tool writes the separator the boundary needs, so that inserted section never runs into the one before it. A missing `---` never blocks a write. A section's extent is still clear, because the `##` heading already marks where every section starts. The prose's unenforced rule that a section "ends at the next `---` line" is replaced by a parse that cannot fold one section into the next. A file that breaks task-format.md's mandatory-separator rule is accepted without anyone being told. The rule then holds only for sections the tool writes, and a malformed hand edit is never surfaced. If a missing `---` was really a sign of a bad paste (half a section, or two merged ones), the tool moves or keeps the damaged text as if it were a complete section. Whether the tool also adds the missing `---` to untouched sections depends on the whole-file-rewrite-or-splice axis, which a sibling question owns.

The tool parses the same way as the silent tolerant reading: an unterminated section ends at the next `##` heading or the end of the file. The write still succeeds with exit 0, but the tool also prints one advisory line on stderr naming each unterminated section's heading and file, so the runner can pass it on to the user. Writes are never blocked, and the malformed hand edit is still made visible, so it gets noticed and fixed without stopping a completion run. The tool's shared contract says a mutator prints nothing on success, and this option breaks it. Runtime prose and the chained shell calls would need a rule for an exit-0 call that still prints output. The `complete-task` agent and the batched calls would have to pass that line through or decide to drop it, which brings back exactly the per-call judgment the tool exists to remove.

open-question.question: Does the task-list tool refuse a write that would leave two sections with the same folded title in one task file (an insert or append of a title TASKS_TODO.md already holds, or a move into a TASKS_DONE.md already holding an entry of that title), or does it write what it is given and leave title uniqueness to the authoring prose as today?
open-question.recommendation: Uniqueness is load-bearing only in TASKS_TODO.md, where the move locates a section by its heading, and this form refuses at authoring time before any work is spent while the move itself gains no failure mode; the within-each-file and cross-file forms refuse a finished task at the move or forbid legitimate follow-up work under a reused title, and writing as given leaves the one property the move depends on unchecked.
open-question.alternative: The tool refuses, with one Error: line and both files unchanged, any insert or append (initialize-then-append in derive-tasks included) whose folded title equals a section TASKS_TODO.md already holds; a move into TASKS_DONE.md is never checked against existing done entries, and no cross-file check is made at authoring time. Guards exactly the file where uniqueness is load-bearing — the completion procedure locates a pending task by its heading in TASKS_TODO.md — and refuses at authoring time, before any work has been done on the task, while the move, the step that runs after a task's work is finished, gains no failure mode of its own. TASKS_DONE.md can end up holding two entries of one title (a task re-submitted after its first copy completed), so the done log stops being keyed by title for any reader that looks an entry up by heading, such as capture or ask-in-milestone-context; a refused append also has to be handled inside derive-tasks' write call, whose shape the sibling question on derive append granularity owns.

The tool enforces no title uniqueness on any write: insert, append, and move write the section they are given whatever titles the target file already holds, and uniqueness stays an authoring duty of the prose alone (task-format.md's "unique within the file" guideline, submit-task's duplicate triage, derive-tasks' skip of work already in TASKS_DONE.md), with no check added now or planned for later. Smallest tool with no new refusal path or test surface, and it guards against a failure that has not occurred: a scan of all 46 milestone directories finds no folded title repeated within any TASKS_TODO.md or TASKS_DONE.md and none present in both files of one milestone, so the prose has held so far. A duplicate the prose misses is written silently and only surfaces later, at completion, where two sections answer the same title and the move takes whichever the matching rule resolves (or refuses then, after the task's work is already done); the goal makes the tool the sole writer, yet the one structural property the move depends on stays unchecked by it. How harmful this is depends on the sibling question on the title matching rule.

The tool refuses, with one Error: line and both files unchanged, any write that would leave two sections of the same folded title in one task file: an insert or append of a title TASKS_TODO.md already holds, and a move into a TASKS_DONE.md already holding an entry of that title; a new TODO title that only matches a done entry is not checked at authoring time. Makes "unique within the file" a property both task files hold by construction, one symmetric rule stated once in the tool and pinned by tests, so every reader of either file can key a section by its title without trusting the authoring prose. A title already present in TASKS_DONE.md passes the authoring check and is then refused at the move, after the completer has done the work and derived the bar, leaving a finished task stuck in TASKS_TODO.md with no tool path to rename it; the runner's recovery from that refusal (and whether the agent may retitle the section) has to be written into the completion prose.

The tool refuses, with one Error: line and both files unchanged, an insert or append whose folded title equals a section in either TASKS_TODO.md or TASKS_DONE.md, and also refuses a move into a TASKS_DONE.md already holding an entry of that title, so one title names at most one section across the milestone's two task files. Catches every collision at authoring time, before any work is spent, including a re-submission of an already completed task's title, so the move-time refusal can only fire on files a writer outside the tool has disturbed and both files stay keyed by title. Widest check: insert and append must read and parse TASKS_DONE.md too, so a malformed done file (an unterminated section, whose handling the sibling question on unterminated sections owns) can now block authoring a new task, and it refuses a deliberate re-run of a completed task under its old title, forcing the author to invent a distinguishing title for legitimate follow-up work.

open-question.question: Beyond refusing an empty title or body, does the task-list tool validate an authored section against task-format.md (title of 4 to 8 title-cased words, a 1 to 3 sentence body, no sub-heading or labeled section inside the body), or does it accept any body text as the section's prose and leave the format to the authoring skills?

open-question.recommendation: Both file contents are rendered before either replace, so restoring the first on a failed second keeps the shared contract that every failure leaves the files unchanged, which the chained git step and an ordinary retry both rely on; the superset forms add a stated exception and leave a state needing hand repair or a detection rule that can misfire, for a second same-directory replace that almost never fails and whose rollback is a few lines exercised by a monkeypatched replace in the tests.
open-question.alternative: The move renders both new file contents in memory before touching either, replaces TASKS_DONE.md first and TASKS_TODO.md second through the existing same-directory temporary-file writer, and if the second replace fails it writes TASKS_DONE.md's original bytes back through the same writer, so the call ends with one Error: line, exit 1, and both files byte-for-byte as they were. Only if that restore also fails does the superset (entry in TASKS_DONE.md, section still in TASKS_TODO.md) remain, and the Error: line then says so. A re-run after a clean failure is an ordinary move. Keeps the tools' shared contract intact without an exception: every failure leaves the files unchanged, exactly as open_questions.py and define_milestone.py promise and test_contract.py pins, so a retry of the chained call needs no repair step and the runner's git step, chained behind the tool, never sees a half-moved pair. Adds a rollback path the other tools never needed (each writes one file), which is hard to exercise in tests without injecting a failure between the two replaces, and its guarantee still degrades to the superset on a double failure, so the contract has to name that edge anyway.

The move renders both new contents first, then replaces TASKS_DONE.md (entry with its Verified bar appended) before TASKS_TODO.md (section removed), mirroring the answer core's fold-before-remove; if the second replace fails it leaves the superset in place with no rollback and prints one Error: line naming that TASKS_DONE.md was written and TASKS_TODO.md was not, exit 1. The tool's every-failure-leaves-files-unchanged contract gains this one stated exception; recovery is left to the runner or the user (removing the duplicate by hand or restoring TASKS_DONE.md from git), and a retried move gets no special handling. The simplest code with a failure state that never loses work: the section and the derived bar both survive on disk, the order matches the fold-before-remove precedent the project already reasons with, and the chained git step does not run, so nothing half-moved is staged or committed. Breaks the uniform unchanged-on-failure contract with a per-subcommand exception, and a straightforward retry would append a second entry of the same title to TASKS_DONE.md or be refused, depending on how the task-title-uniqueness sibling settles, so the interrupted state needs a manual repair before the task can be recorded again.

The same DONE-first, TODO-second order with no rollback and the same Error: line on a failed second replace, plus a resume rule: when a move is called for a title whose section still stands in TASKS_TODO.md and whose entry already stands in TASKS_DONE.md, the tool treats the earlier move as interrupted and completes it by removing the section from TASKS_TODO.md only, keeping the existing DONE entry and its bar rather than writing the newly piped one. The interrupted state heals by simply re-running the same chained call, so neither the runner nor the user ever hand-edits a task file, and no work is lost at any point. Adds a second code path and a detection rule that can misfire when a TASKS_DONE.md entry of the same folded title is not actually this task's interrupted move, and silently drops the re-run's freshly piped bar; its safety depends on how the task-title-uniqueness and task-title-matching siblings settle, since both govern what counts as the same title.

open-question.question: Does the new tool repeat the stdin reader, ToolError, the one-Error-line main, and the atomic same-directory writer as its own standalone single file, as define_milestone.py does with a parity test that it imports neither sibling, or do the three tools now share one helper module under core/tools/ that the build copies beside them?
open-question.recommendation: It follows the define_milestone.py precedent exactly: no change to the two working tools or the build, every rendered tool stays one runnable file copied byte-identical into each host, and no run imports a sibling, which matters because the build's check walks every file under a host tree and would report a __pycache__ written by a sibling import as not produced by the build; the shared-module and import forms refactor live tools inside a milestone about the task files, the inlining form gives the build its first code transform, and the drift test pins source shape rather than behaviour.
open-question.alternative: The new task-list tool is one self-contained file carrying its own copies of the stdin reader, ToolError, the one-Error-line main with its describe/fail path, and the same-directory atomic writer, written for its own needs (keeping the target's mode, as open_questions.py does, since it rewrites existing files). open_questions.py and define_milestone.py stay untouched. The parity precedent is extended: a test asserts the new tool imports neither sibling, and its conformance to the shared output contract is pinned only behaviourally by its own subprocess tests, with no check that the copies match the siblings' text. A later milestone may still extract a module; this one does not. Follows the established define_milestone.py precedent exactly: no change to the two working tools or to the build, every rendered tool stays one runnable file copied byte-identical into each host, and running a tool never imports a sibling, so no __pycache__ directory is written beside the tools in core/tools or in a live hosts tree that build_hosts.py --check walks file by file. A third copy of roughly a hundred lines of contract plumbing, already diverging between the two existing tools (define_milestone.py's writer takes the default mode, open_questions.py's keeps the target's), so a later contract change has to be made three times and nothing but the behavioural tests notices a copy left behind.

The new tool is a self-contained file with its own copies of the stdin reader, ToolError, the one-Error-line main, and the atomic writer, and imports neither sibling, as above; in addition a new test parses the three tool sources and asserts that the named shared helpers (those the three can hold identically, such as ToolError, fold, the stdin reader, describe, the fail path, and main's exception ladder) are textually or AST-identical across every tool that defines them, harmonizing the existing copies where they differ in wording only. Helpers that legitimately differ, such as the two writers' mode handling, are either harmonized into one mode-keeping writer or left out of the identity check by name. Keeps every tool a standalone file with no build or import change while turning silent drift of the duplicated plumbing into a failing test, so the duplication cost is paid once in the test rather than remembered at every later contract change. Adds a source-shape test of a kind the suite does not yet have, which pins how the code is written rather than what it does, and it touches define_milestone.py and open_questions.py to bring their copies into identity, widening a milestone scoped to the task files into a cross-tool tidy.

A new stdlib-only module under core/tools/ (one file, no placeholder, naming no host) holds ToolError, fold, the stdin reader, describe, the one-Error-line main wrapper, and the same-directory atomic writer (with the mode choice as a parameter). The new tool, define_milestone.py, and open_questions.py all import it as a sibling module, relying on the script's own directory being on sys.path when invoked as python3 <plugin root>/tools/<tool>.py; the build copies it beside them unchanged into every host's tools directory, and the define parity test's no-import assertion is replaced by one asserting each tool imports only the helper module. Each tool sets bytecode writing off before the import (or the build and --check skip __pycache__), so running a tool leaves no cache directory in core/tools or a hosts tree. One copy of the output contract and the write path for all three tools, so the contract the CLAUDE.md invariants describe lives in one place and a fix or change to it lands once for every tool, and the new tool is smaller. Refactors both existing, well-tested tools inside a milestone about the task files, adds a fourth file under tools/ that every host tree carries, and introduces a cross-file runtime dependency: a tool run from a partial copy or with the plugin directory off sys.path fails on import, and without the bytecode guard a single run writes a __pycache__ directory that build_hosts.py --check reports as not produced by the build.

No helper module is added: the new tool imports ToolError, the stdin reader, the error-reporting main path, and the atomic writer directly from the existing open_questions.py sibling, which stays the de facto home of the shared contract; define_milestone.py stays standalone with its existing no-import parity test, and the new tool gets a test asserting it imports only open_questions. Reuses the one tool whose contract is already pinned by test_contract.py without creating any new file or touching define_milestone.py, so the new tool inherits the exact error and write behaviour of the established sole writer at the smallest change. Couples the task-list tool to the 1,270-line XML tool, which every task-list call then parses and loads, so a change made to open_questions.py for its own document can break task writes; it carries the same sibling-import and __pycache__ exposure as a shared module, and it leaves the three tools on two different sharing models.

The shared helpers live once in a module under core/tools/, which each tool's source imports so the core files and the test suite (pythonpath core/tools) work as they are, but the build renders each tool with the helper's source inlined in place of the import, so every rendered tool in every host tree is again one standalone file and the helper module itself is either not shipped or shipped unused. All three tools adopt it, and a check confirms each rendered tool runs without its sibling. One source of the contract plumbing for maintainers while every installed tool remains a self-contained file with no runtime sibling import and no __pycache__ written in the host tree. Gives the generic build its first code-transforming step for tools, ending the byte-identical copy of core/tools into each host, and the test suite exercises the import form rather than the rendered form users run, so a rendering fault in the inlining reaches users untested unless a new rendered-tool test is added.
